children: Russia loaded more than 30M barrels of crude oil onto tankers last week, the most since late July, as Ukraine ramped up its attacks on the country’s refineries, forcing producers to divert crude intended for those plants into export streams, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.
The 39 tankers that loaded Russian crude in the week ending November 15 carried 30.2M barrels, up from 23.6M barrels on 31 ships the previous week, according to Bloomberg's vessel-tracking data.
On a four-week average through November 15, overseas flows rose to 3.9M bbl/day, their highest since late July and up 280K bbl/day from the period to November 8.
Ukraine has attacked 13 Russian refineries since the start of November, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, including the TAIF-NK facility in Nizhnekamsk and the Ilsky refinery in southern Russia.
President Zelenskyy claimed over the weekend that Ukraine had disabled more that 55% of Russian oil refining capacity through its campaign.

The attacks have complicated Russia's plans to increase diesel production under its October agreement with President Trump, with more crude leaving Russia unrefined, while the diesel deal itself has encountered problems, failing to find buyers for any of the U.S. cargoes, which are now being offered to fuel distributors in Brazil.

The surge in crude shipments has not translated into higher earnings for the Russian exports, as the four-week average value of Russian seaborne crude exports fell to $2.45B per week, a seven-week low, with the increase in total flows more than offset by a fifth straight weekly drop in prices for Russia's flagship Urals crude.
Crude oil futures settled modestly higher Tuesday, as the market balanced renewed fighting in the Middle East against signs of recovering supplies.

U.S. warplanes struck Iranian missile launch sites on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf after Iran targeted Bahrain for the third time in less than a week, and President Trump said the U.S. is investigating a report about potential Iranian plans to target Washington, D.C.
U.S. forces launched limited attacks on Qeshm Island earlier this month, saying they were designed to help tankers and other vessels make safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Still, the International Energy Agency, Goldman Sachs, and other groups have flagged a shift to a global oil surplus.

"Periodic flareups in the Persian Gulf have been a fact of life throughout the past nine months, and, generally speaking, their effect on oil prices has diminished over time," Raymond James analyst Pavel Molchanov said in a note. "The oil market has become acclimated to these episodes, just as long as there is no return to all-out war."
